entries.title: Jacaranda by Gaël Faye review – the limits of forgiveness after Rwanda
entries.summary: This bold family saga explores a search for healing and truth in the aftermath of the Rwanda genocideHow to forgive the unforgivable? How to live in the aftermath of atrocity? entries.content:
How to forgive the unforgivable? How to live in the aftermath of atrocity? Following 2016’s Small Country, French-Rwandan rapper and writer Gaël Faye takes on huge questions in his second novel, Jacaranda, which explores the seismic events of the Rwanda genocide and the aftershocks that continue to ripple through the generations.

Structurally bold, the story opens in summer 1994 with Milan, Faye’s then 12-year-old protagonist, enjoying an extended break from school. Milan’s father is white French and the family’s life in Versailles is the embodiment of first world ease – their holiday that year, as usual, spent sailing at the Île de Ré. Milan’s mother, though, is Rwandan. Venancia arrived in the 1970s, establishing a life for herself, a successful clothing boutique, a family. However, she cannot share the French ease, much less her thoughts on the disturbing reports from Rwanda now making the evening news.

Indeed, taciturn Venancia has never shared the reasons she left for Europe, and Milan only learns he has extended Rwandan family when his “cousin” Claude arrives at the end of the holidays, out of the blue, and terribly injured by a machete. Small and so traumatised he can barely speak, Claude has been brought to France for treatment. While Venancia takes him in under obligation, young Milan quickly takes him to heart, and the boys’ developing bond over the autumn is tenderly described. But once his wounds are improving, Claude returns as abruptly as he arrived, and with just as little explanation, and the hole he leaves in Milan’s life refuses to heal.

In part two we jump to 1998. Milan is 16, his parents’ marriage is faltering, and so are his studies, and he travels to Rwanda for the first time. In Kigali, Milan finds an alternative mother figure in Eusébie, a childhood friend of Venancia’s. A fellow Tutsi, and a survivor of the 1994 genocide, she is now a campaigner for justice and healing. The jacaranda of the title grows in her garden, providing shade for her elderly mother Rosalie and her newborn daughter Stella, the sibling Milan has been craving. When he holds the child, she smiles her first smile.

Much to his joy, Milan also finds Claude again, and through him meets the pivotal character Sartre, who lives in Le Palais, a ramshackle compound far from Eusébie’s leafy neighbourhood. Here, at the height of the violence, he gave shelter to dozens of Tutsi children, orphans of the genocide, becoming a Fagin of sorts. A scavenger of considerable discernment, Sartre has established an extensive library of books and music; Milan learns much about Rwanda under his tutelage, and from the many now almost-adult orphans – not least that, here, he is considered white. He finds a home from home among them regardless. Having stared death in the face, the young residents of Le Palais spend their days grafting and their nights partying, and Milan is inspired by their defiance.

His grandmother is less welcoming. Milan finds Mamie much like Venancia: withheld and withholding. But he does begin to see that the 1994 violence had long and tangled roots, as does the Hutu-Tutsi divide; Claude was not the first in their family to suffer, but exactly why and how they fled remains shrouded.

Milan will return to Rwanda many more times, and for longer and longer periods. Adrift, he will seek out Sartre, and the oblivion of partying in Le Palais; in search of shelter, he will turn to Eusébie and the now grown Stella; under the shade of the jacaranda, he will discover that she seeks answers too.

The book’s most painful chapters describe the gacaca courts, which ran until 2012: mass open-air hearings, gathering testimonies from across the victim-perpetrator divide; public confessions and accusations that campaigners like Eusébie hoped would provide truth and reconciliation.

But some truths are hard to take – perhaps impossible – and in some revelations, Milan sees forgiveness reach its limits. Venancia will not be the only one to have withheld her story, and neither will Claude have been alone in masquerading as someone he’s not. Who can Milan trust after all that he’s heard? Where can he find peace when even the shade of the jacaranda will not provide refuge?

In Milan and his family, in Claude, Stella, Sartre and Eusébie, Faye gives face and voice to the human capacity for endurance. Perhaps above all, he sees the harm in the divides we make between victim and perpetrator, Tutsi and Hutu, parent and child, black and white, Europe and Africa. Jacaranda is a bold and uncompromising book.

entries.title: What we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in July
entries.summary: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsI recently read Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot. entries.content:
Max Porter, writer

I recently read Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot. It’s one of the best novels I’ve ever read about what it means to live with others, or decide not to; what we owe the people we love, the natural world, and ourselves. I also really enjoyed Robert Frost, by Robert Frost and Stacy Skolnik. It’s not that Robert Frost; it’s an itinerant young American Robert Frost who jots down his thoughts and observations on homelessness, food, value, music, drugs, the philosophical wastelands of contemporary life, and Stacy Skolnik has turned them into these delightful, oddly profound, poems. Also, coming soon, End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. Everyone should read it. It tells us exactly what’s going on.

Max Porter is the author of books including Shy and Grief Is the Thing With Feathers

Richard, Guardian reader

I am reading Headlights by the American horror writer CJ Leede. This is her third novel. I think she has the potential to be the 21st century’s Stephen King – she’s that good! Headlights is a pitch-black horror novel with overtones of Silence of the Lambs and Osgood Perkins’ fabulous film Longlegs. It is also a love letter to King’s The Shining and has a strong environmental message too, concerning man’s uneasy and destructive relationship with the natural world. Leede is such a wonderful writer of prose. Her characters are three-dimensional and you care about them almost immediately (which makes what she does to some of them all the more horrible!). She has an obvious love of the American landscape and describes it beautifully, and the book’s relationship with The Shining will have horror lovers squealing with delight – there are little Easter eggs peppered throughout the book.

Daisy Johnson, writer

Lately I am to be found loudly and excitedly recommending The Corner That Held Them by Sylvia Townsend Warner, first published in 1948. Set over 200 years and taking in the Black Death, the Great Revolt of 1381 and much bickering, the novel follows a convent of nuns living in the British Fenlands. I’ve also loved reading The Empusium, an equally claustrophobic book by Olga Tokarczuk which, thrillingly, is described as “a health resort horror story” on the cover. It follows a young man with failing health who visits a sanatorium in the mountains to recover. It is a rather glorious and surreal romp.

Long Wave by Daisy Johnson is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

Sarah, Guardian reader

This month (perhaps not so subconsciously) I seem to have been drawn mostly to both fiction and nonfiction featuring women facing personal challenges. In fiction, Tamarin by Priya Hein and Under Water by Tara Menon have been favourites this month, and I think the books pair well together: both feature women who return to their homeland after life-changing experiences. In nonfiction, My Cantopop Nights by Emma-Lee Moss was a thoroughly enjoyable read about one woman’s search to find home and her identity in Hong Kong. Her experiences of motherhood resonated with me, and I was transported back to my own time spent in Hong Kong a decade ago. Finally, a hybrid of the two genres: Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa. I devoured this book, which vividly brings to life the stories of a number of women who inhabited a psychiatric hospital in Ireland in the 1890s and early 20th century, the result of obsessive research by the author.

Avni Doshi, writer

While researching for my next novel, in which one of the characters is an artist, I came across a brilliant book called Colour by Victoria Finlay. Finlay dives deep into the fascinating history of where colour comes from. It reads like an adventure into the painter’s palette. Expect intrigue, beetles and dead bodies. Andrea Bajani’s The Anniversary was also a recent favourite. The story follows a grown man unpicking the web of his painful childhood. A slim book written in crisp prose, there isn’t a word out of place. I read it in one sitting. I also loved and have been widely recommending A Splintering by Dur e Aziz Amna, in which a cunning and ambitious woman from a village in Pakistan reshapes the future that was set for her. Rarely have I read a character so ruthless and irresistible. Her hunger growls on the page.

entries.title: Jacqueline Crooks: ‘Toni Morrison’s voice made me want to find my own’
entries.summary: The novelist on learning empathy from Charles Dickens, the playfulness of Irenosen Okojie and avoiding Jane AustenMy earliest reading memory I was eight when I was given The Water-Babies by Charles Kingsley, after being moved from my grand­mother’s care to live with my mother and her husband, who I barely knew. The story is about leaving one world, adapting to another. Surviving. It gave shape to
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

I was eight when I was given The Water-Babies by Charles Kingsley, after being moved from my grand­mother’s care to live with my mother and her husband, who I barely knew. The story is about leaving one world, adapting to another. Surviving. It gave shape to unnamed feelings and developed my survival imagination: imagining beyond my circumstances.

My favourite book growing up

David Copperfield by Charles Dickens. I followed David’s journey from exclusion to belonging. Dickens vivifies his characters; you grow alongside them. The novel taught me empathy, and that some relationships sustain us while others must be left behind.

The book that changed me as a teenager

I read Wuthering Heights when I was 12 or 13. Heathcliff fascinates me: enigmatic, brooding, never fully explained. Emily Brontë taught me landscape is character. The moors are a living force, mirroring Cathy and Heathcliff’s emotional lives. That shaped my writing: I’m drawn to unknowable characters and psychologically alive places.

The writer who changed my mind

I was in my 40s when a writing tutor suggested I read The Tempest while writing my story collection The Ice Migration. The island setting, themes of displacement and longing for return resonated, and made me realise Shakespeare could speak to my life.

The author who made me want to be a writer

I can’t remember which Toni Morrison novel affected me most: The Bluest Eye, Tar Baby or Jazz. Her worlds are familiar, dreamlike, grounded yet on the edge of the unknowable. Morrison showed me that Black lives and characters from marginalised worlds are worthy of being centred within literature. Her voice made me want to find my own.

The book or author I came back to

When I first read Wilson Harris, his writing felt demanding. Returning to it in my 40s, I was captivated by his Guyanese landscapes. Harris showed me landscape can carry history, memory, imagination. I learned to value my cultural inheritance and bring Jamaica’s landscapes on to the page.

The book I reread

I first read Irenosen Okojie’s Nudibranch in 2019 and return to it often. She does extraordinary things with language and image; at times, the writing creates its own imaginative vocabulary. It is a masterclass in inventiveness, playfulness and creative courage.

The book I could never read again

Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. I studied it at school. I’ve always questioned respectability politics. The world of courtship and dinner parties feels confining. I respect Austen’s skill, but I’m drawn to books about characters who cross boundaries, venture into the unknown rather than finding their place within the social order.

The book I discovered later in life

I discovered Xiaolu Guo’s Radical in 2023. What struck me was its freedom. Guo combines memoir, philosophy, visual art and language, using Chinese script to guide the reader. I admire its fierce independence: a woman stepping outside prescribed roles to pursue creativity on her own terms. Guo isn’t writing to be liked; she is writing to push boundaries.

The book I am currently reading

I’m reading Cosmic Music: The Life, Art and Transcendence of Alice Coltrane by Andy Beta. Coltrane’s music has long been a muse for my writing and influenced my new novel, Sky City. Her music is spiritual, hopeful. As a writer, books about music help me to listen for rhythm and pace.

My comfort read

There’s something deeply reassuring about returning to Walter Mosley’s Always Outnumbered, Always Outgunned. And Socrates Fortlow is so familiar, he feels like family. His resourcefulness, humour and care for others, even in the face of hardship, remind me of people I’ve known throughout my life. I always come away believing that kindness, dignity and transformation are still possible, no matter what is going on in the world.

entries.title: The best recent poetry – review roundup
entries.summary: Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton; The Channel by Jana Prikryl; Stepmother by Helen Mort; Drunken Driving by Martina EvansSmall Birds Singing by Matthew Welton (Carcanet, £12.99)Written in unrhymed couplets that shrink and grow across the page like a concertina going through its scales, Welton’s poems focus attention on the city through the seasons: weeds through concrete, wasps emerging from
entries.content:
Small Birds Singing by Matthew Welton (Carcanet, £12.99)

Written in unrhymed couplets that shrink and grow across the page like a concertina going through its scales, Welton’s poems focus attention on the city through the seasons: weeds through concrete, wasps emerging from the gaps between bricks, frozen towels on a clothesline, the shadows of jackdaws on a lawn. His gaze is neutral, and it often falls on that which we’d normally turn away from, things slightly out of place, or that disturb our sense of propriety: “more cardboard in the recycling bin / than the recycling bin can contain”. This is a poetry of things, like the poetry of Francis Ponge, but as Welton says: “no thinginess without thought”. Welton’s thoughts – though whether they are his or whether they emerge from his surroundings or from the act of writing itself, it is impossible to say – are couched in deliciously riddling couplets: “it is not the habit of patterns / to emphasise the pattern of habits”. He reminds us forcefully that poetry is all around us and within us, that anything can go in a poem: a sandwich, a desiccated lump of duck shit, the pile of junk left outside a house during a refurbishment. Poems can mirror our world in all its messiness, and in doing so let us see it a little bit better.

The Channel by Jana Prikryl (Faber, £12.99

The casual violence of King Lear, the greed, the bureaucracy, and the indifference to human life, make the play particularly resonant to contemporary audiences. In her fourth collection, Prikryl channels the voice of Cordelia to think back through her own family story of displacement from the Czech Republic. Shakespeare’s Lear becomes “a document of fact / of things that happened and keep happening”, enabling Prikryl to explore her own separation from friends and family and her experiences of migration, where home is nowhere. In Dover Calais a ferry trip to France is meshed with the story of Cordelia’s exile, morphing into an account of a ferry disaster which in turn cuts to a scene where refugees make for shore in small boats: “Waves / unreal, and driving rain, the two-year-old / left face-down on a beach nine years ago / came up for me”. Like the scissored-off hospital undershirt in In the Mould, Prikryl’s language cuts off, ending abruptly: “or was the famous sweetness / of grandmother a bluff / which through and through was too”. This rewiring of the sentence creates dazzling leaps of thought, jumping from refugee camps to Shakespeare’s Fool battling with a tsunami of text messages to dissident window cleaners out of the novels of Milan Kundera to tender moments shared with her father. It’s a bold “stepping out of form” that turns its back on the neatness of the lyric, and by doing so creates a new poetic language which, like the language of Calvino in Invisible Cities, is able to connect everything to everything.

Stepmother by Helen Mort (Chatto & Windus, £12.99)

The ubiquity of the stepmother in fairytales has been explained by psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim as enabling the child to keep the image of the good mother intact. Marina Warner reminds us that their presence is historically connected to the high mortality rate of mothers in childbirth, though today women are more likely to find themselves in the role as a result of divorce. Here Mort explores her own experience of this neglected dimension of maternity alongside its representation in myth. “Better a serpent than a stepmother,” said Euripides, and the sentiment is reinforced across a range of stories where we witness stepmothers abandon their children in forests or simply decapitate them to be rid of them once and for all. Mort shows how traditional images of bad stepmothers are perpetuated in news stories and film, but she finds the modern experience repeating history in more subtle ways: she is jealous of her stepdaughter’s figure, distantly echoing the stepmother in Snow White, or, in an inversion of the way Cinderella is treated, it is the stepmother who finds herself pushed to the edge of her own household by photographs of the husband’s first marriage. Mort’s poems are a vivid compendium of stories, but they also offer ways of escaping the trap of myth: “You did not pick your stepchildren. Nor did they pick you. / But every day you can choose to love each other.”

Drunken Driving by Martina Evans (Carcanet, £12.99)

This electrifying sequel to Evans’s 2023 sonnet sequence The Coming Thing is set 10 years on. Imelda, having put the Cork punk scene behind her, is now a young mother, married to Carl, working shifts at Pentonville prison and learning to negotiate the spiderweb crossroads of London in her red Astra. Appropriately for this carceral environment, the sonnets come cuffed with quotations taken from prison protocols, driving manuals and the novel Dracula: “With strained ears, I listened, and heard downstairs the grinding of the key in the great lock and the falling back of the heavy door.” Immediately we are plunged into a world of dangerous driving, vampiric warders, overcrowding and casual racism. Conversation within the prison walls is frowned upon but outside the banter flies between Imelda and her father Justin: “When I said Pentonville was a Chamber / of Horrors, Justin said, You’ve got an imagination. I’ll give you that. / But I don’t need one! I said. Half of Madame Tussaud’s waxworks were / hanged there. Justin snorted, Highly-strung, like yourself?” Pumped up with adrenaline, fuelled by alcohol, and peppered with razor-sharp observations, this reads like Porridge on steroids.

entries.title: Mario Vargas Llosa by Gerald Martin review – the Peruvian leftist who fell in love with Margaret Thatcher
entries.summary: This stylish biography of the author traces his journey from left to right, and from ‘posh Lima’ to Cricklewood“At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Those words on the opening page of Conversation in the Cathedral announced the arrival of a writer who understood that national history could become the organising principle of fiction. At precisely the moment when Latin America was disc
entries.content:
“At what precise moment had Peru fucked itself up?” Those words on the opening page of Conversation in the Cathedral announced the arrival of a writer who understood that national history could become the organising principle of fiction. At precisely the moment when Latin America was discovering the intoxicating possibilities of magical realism – a form whose exuberance had an elective affinity with revolutionary politics, collapsing the distinction between the marvellous and the possible – Mario Vargas Llosa plumped for old-fashioned realism instead.

It was a question of sensibility as much as politics, Gerald Martin suggests in this chatty yet coolly analytical biography. He traces the path of a novelist who began by dissecting oligarchy with surgical precision and ended happily dining among its ranks, completing one of literary history’s most spectacular political migrations – from the hard left to the hard right, over the course of half a century.

Yet Martin’s revisionist point is that Vargas Llosa crossed a shorter ideological distance than is often imagined. He never truly belonged to the left. His brief flirtation was not with socialism so much as with a socialist: the dazzling, unattainable Lea Barba, whom he met at San Marcos University. Their undergraduate comradeship unfolded between bookshops and the smoky tables of a bohemian nightclub managed by Lea’s communist father. Beneath the guerrilla chic, Martin finds in Vargas Llosa an old patrician confidence in hierarchy. The “factory defect”, as one university contemporary put it, was congenital: Vargas Llosa never ceased to be a “Lima posh boy”.

Vargas Llosa’s greatest novels were written under Jean-Paul Sartre’s spell, before the French philosopher’s indulgence towards revolutionary regimes finally alienated him. The break with Sartre in particular and the left in general came in 1971 with the “Padilla affair”, when the Cuban poet Heberto Padilla was arrested and compelled to perform a grotesque public confession renouncing his “counter-revolutionary” work and denouncing fellow dissidents. Vargas Llosa led an international campaign against Castro’s treatment of writers. Martin is strikingly unsentimental about this celebrated moment of liberal courage. He argues that Vargas Llosa’s comparison of Castro with Stalin was wildly overdrawn and that the campaign against Havana helped isolate the regime at precisely the moment the Latin American left most needed it.

Many biographies are now exercises in rehabilitation. Happily, Martin has written a genuinely critical life. The occasional overworked oedipal reading of his subject’s affairs and an inexplicable fondness for the word “sexy” are minor irritants in a searching, stylish account whose real subject is not merely Vargas Llosa but the intellectual and political milieux that made and unmade him.

Martin restores the women whom Vargas Llosa reduced to literary raw material. His scandalous marriage at 19 to his aunt-by-marriage, Julia Urquidi, 10 years his senior, became Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter – the sunniest, and by some distance the best loved, of his novels. Her own memoir, What Varguitas Didn’t Say exposes the gap between Vargas Llosa’s breezy romance and the less charming reality of adultery and abandonment. Alas, it never troubled the bestseller lists.

Julia was discarded for Patricia Llosa, his first cousin, nine years his junior, with whom he had three children. Like so many writers’ wives of her generation, she was forever taking one for the team, quietly spiriting away the offending pram whenever he bellowed: “Patriiiicia! Take this baby away, I can’t woooork!”

Half a century later, she too was replaced, this time by the Spanish society doyenne Isabel Preysler, the mother of the singer Enrique Iglesias, with whom the octogenarian finally exchanged the republic of letters for the pages of ¡Hola!.

His move to England proved unexpectedly formative. Vargas Llosa settled in unswinging Cricklewood, which suited a pre-existing taste for suburban conservatism. The historian Hugh Thomas, another distinguished émigré from the left, played Virgil to Vargas Llosa’s Dante, escorting him into the circles of Tory respectability and, eventually, to Margaret Thatcher herself. He wrote up the encounter with fanboy adoration in a piece titled The Lady Among the Wild Beasts.

The novelist who spent decades exposing the seductions of ideology proved remarkably susceptible to a new one. After Peru rejected his presidential ambitions when he ran on a neoliberal ticket against Alberto Fujimori in 1990, he increasingly revelled in precisely those circles where power congratulates itself upon its realism. Utopias, sources of aspiration on the left, became mere pathologies in his later fictions.

After the 2010 Nobel prize, Vargas Llosa increasingly lent his prestige to the hard right, backing Peru’s trigger-happy unelected ruler Dina Boluarte and Chile’s anti-gay, anti-abortion crusader José Antonio Kast; denouncing feminism as literature’s “staunchest enemy,” and treating every leftward electoral twitch as a “return to caudillismo.”

Gabriel García Márquez is the book’s foil: the magician to Vargas Llosa’s realist, the man who stayed with the leftist tribe while his lesser rival abandoned it. Martin, now the biographer of both, is uniquely placed to reconstruct the most famous right hook in literary history. In 1976, Vargas Llosa floored García Márquez with a punch after allegedly accusing him of overstepping the mark by comforting Patricia during the collapse of their marriage.

The punch marked more than a personal rupture. It sealed an ideological one. García Márquez later remarked that there were only “two soups on the menu”: capitalism and socialism. Vargas Llosa turned up his nose at one and spent the rest of his life gorging himself on the other.

entries.title: Helm by Sarah Hall audiobook review – a breath of fresh air from the Pennines
entries.summary: Louise Brealey teases out the playful and poetic moments of these shapeshifting stories, told from the perspective of the northeasterly wind and those it has wreaked chaos on through the agesThe only named wind in the British Isles, Helm is a strong northeasterly gale that blows down the slopes of Cross Fell in the Pennines and is known for its unusual cloud formations. Helm has been known to disl
entries.content:
The only named wind in the British Isles, Helm is a strong northeasterly gale that blows down the slopes of Cross Fell in the Pennines and is known for its unusual cloud formations. Helm has been known to dislodge roofs, haystacks, trees and riders from their horses.

Twenty years in the writing, Sarah Hall’s Helm is an ambitious novel that tells stories from the perspective of the wind, and from the people on whom, through the ages, Helm has wreaked chaos. Those figures include a Neolithic tribeswoman and seer called NaNay who is building a stone circle; an astrologer and exorcist known as a “wizard priest”; a Victorian meteorologist who travels across the Pennines by train and later by carriage into Helm’s “onslaught”; and a climatologist measuring microplastics in the atmosphere from her observation hut in the fells. Separated by centuries, their stories are nonetheless woven together, each of them bonded by weather.

Helm is a book of vast scope, lyrical prose and sharp shifts in style and tone, all of which makes it a tricky job for a narrator. Fortunately, the actor Louise Brealey – who has already read two of Hall’s books: The Wolf Border and Burntcoat – proves more than able, teasing out its playful and poetic moments and revelling in the flashes of coarseness.

Helm is a slippery, shapeshifting phenomenon that Hall notes can be hard to visualise and explain, though that doesn’t stop her from trying. “Imagine a skater launching off a quarter pipe two-thousand feet high, then somersaulting. Again. And again. And again.”

Available via Faber, 13hr 3min

Further listening

Whistler

Ann Patchett, Bloomsbury, 10hr 43min

A fiftysomething English teacher notices an older man following her around New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and eventually recognises him as her former stepfather, Eddie. As they reconnect, old memories come to the surface. Read by the author.

London Falling

Patrick Radden Keefe, Picador, 12hr 59min

Blending true crime and social history, the Empire of Pain author unravels the knotty story of a troubled teenager’s death by falling from a building into the River Thames.

entries.title: Beginning Middle End by Valeria Luiselli review – a mother and daughter’s odyssey
entries.summary: This journey of discovery from the US to Sicily tackles urgent themes, but is increasingly inward-lookingIn Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.
entries.content:
In Grace Paley’s short story A Conversation With My Father, a request is made of the Paley-like narrator. “I would like you to write a simple story just once more,” her father says, “the kind Maupassant wrote, or Chekhov … Just recognisable people and then write down what happened to them next.” Her attempt, and its failure to impress him, is the action that powers the story. Valeria Luiselli’s fourth novel is propelled by a similar request, the daughter of the Luiselli-like narrator asking: “Will you finally write a novel with a beginning, a middle, and an end?” It’s a problem Luiselli has addressed before. In her 2017 book-length essay about undocumented migrant children, Tell Me How It Ends, she writes that the difficulty in telling their story “is that it has no beginning, no middle and no end”.

Beginning Middle End charts the narrator’s efforts to corral life into a narrative. The father in Paley’s story would be similarly unimpressed. After a “slow, entangled” divorce, the narrator, a Mexican living in the United States, embarks on a European book tour with her 12-year-old daughter. She has a coil removed in Munich; her daughter loses a tooth in Prague; near Amsterdam they watch children learning to swim with their shoes on in case of floods. When summer comes, the pair fly to Catania in Sicily. The narrator’s grandmother grew up nearby. They stay in the apartment of a pianist who’s away on tour, with whom the narrator had a “brief and feverish encounter” the previous year.

This book can be made to sound dense with plot: Etna is erupting. Wildfires rage. The narrator’s mother, in Baja California, might be developing dementia and is possibly planning an act of eco-terrorism. Before the narrator left for Europe her mother gave her a valuable heirloom, a Roman mosaic tile portraying the god Proteus; the narrator’s grandmother took it from an excavation site before leaving Sicily.

Mother and daughter discuss Proteus’s appearance in the Odyssey, their explorations of myth and classical literature becoming a central strand. The narrator’s daughter grows obsessed with returning the mosaic to the ruined villa it came from.

After a few weeks the pianist returns, the narrator’s attraction to him rapidly eroding as the sex gets rough, he fights with her daughter, and neglects to help when she gets stung by jellyfish. Yet despite all this, the novel has trouble gathering momentum – or perhaps isn’t interested in doing so. Paley’s narrator calls plot “the absolute line between two points which I’ve always despised”. Luiselli’s seems to feel the same way, breaking her narrative into discrete little segments like the tesserae from which Proteus’s face emerges.

Throughout, the narrator questions what she is writing. “I don’t have a clear idea about what I am doing, or what will happen next, not yet,” she admits. “I get entangled in possible beginnings, intricate plots, improvised premises.” Later she wonders if this project isn’t a novel at all but an essay. “Perhaps the middle does not fit into the tighter architecture of a novel, the corset of plot. The middle feels more akin to the distracted, loose, meandering spirit of essaying. Maybe it will have to be an essay until it can be a novel again, an essay with a beginning, a middle, and an end.” This persistent identity crisis is only resolved when the daughter eventually seizes control of the narrative.

Luiselli’s writing has always been essayistic and self-reflexive. In fact, she began in 2010 as an essayist with the lyrical, literary Sidewalks. Her first novel, Faces in the Crowd, blended autofiction and metafiction – the book portraying its own construction, just as Beginning Middle End does – with a fictionalised account of the life of a real Mexican poet. Her second, The Story of My Teeth, is also partly about its own construction: in an author’s note Luiselli explains how the book was created in tandem with a group of factory workers. In a Sebaldian touch, photographs accompany the text.

In many ways Beginning Middle End mirrors Luiselli’s previous novel, 2019’s Lost Children Archive, itself a fictional expansion of Tell Me How It Ends. Its narration is shared between an unnamed woman, whose marriage is collapsing, and her stepson, who addresses his part to his stepsister. In Beginning Middle End the unnamed narrator’s marriage has ended, and her daughter writes postcards to her stepbrother. In both books the text is divided into short, titled chapters that prefer essayistic thought to the construction of dramatic scenes. Both children come into possession of Polaroid cameras, their pictures providing wordless conclusions to each novel. There is another explicit link, one that paradoxically divides the books’ narrators, but revealing it would be a spoiler.

The larger contradiction within Luiselli’s work is that although the subjects it returns to – the role and status of the mother, migration, the climate crisis – are universal and urgent, it is becoming ever more inward-looking. The most dramatic journey Beginning Middle End describes is whether it can succeed in becoming the book we hold in our hands. In a knowing moment, the narrator’s daughter studies the mosaic of Proteus – a shapeshifter, just like this novel – “as if she were looking into a mirror or a pool of water, like a little Narcissus peering at himself”. Since finishing the book, it’s the image that has persisted most strongly in my memory.

entries.content:
The AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term.

The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too.

Drage, an assistant research professor at the University of Cambridge’s Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence, has conducted research that debunks AI-powered recruitment processes, and exposes the dangers of incorporating AI into law enforcement. Many of her criticisms of big tech will be familiar: that AI algorithms perpetuate and entrench pre-existing biases; that for all their bland, generic promises to be “transparent” and “accountable”, tech giants have become too big to care about ethics; that a handful of executives have amassed far too much power; and that the rollout of AI is happening without our consent and without consideration for planetary health. But her writing has intellectual heft, and her philosophical explorations of, for example, how we define intelligence and why this matters, are very interesting.

Occasionally, however, Drage’s arguments seem rushed and become sloppy. “It’s merely an illusion that the labour force is disappearing: work is simply shifting, from artists to data labellers and from marketeers to engineers,” she writes at one point. But it’s not clear that artists and “marketeers” will become redundant in the coming AI era. It’s also not as though the data labellers working for poverty wages in Kenya would have been artists 10 years ago. Equally, given the importance she rightly places on promoting diversity in AI, it’s disappointing that she dismisses unconscious bias as “merely another way of taking the perspective of the perpetrator rather than the recipient of harm”, as though intention is completely irrelevant. She writes that people are ready for “less placid” conversations about equality, I’d add that these conversations also demand accuracy and nuance.

The book’s title suggests Drage wants to offer an alternative vision of what AI could be. She gives a few examples of the kind of ethical, community-based AI projects she thinks should be replacing top-down big tech products, and many of them are strangely underwhelming. They include an app called Mumkin designed to facilitate difficult conversations about female genital mutilation (FGM) in India, and Kuini, an AI chatbot built to help Māori women quit smoking. In both instances I found myself wondering what value AI brings to these endeavours – particularly given all that Drage has discussed about its environmental impact and exploitative supply chains. Is an app more effective than training community members to act as counsellors, or funding support groups and peer support workers?

Drage describes a toolkit she co-designed to help AI companies act ethically and comply with EU regulations as a “cornerstone of utopianism”, because it shifts the focus on to how AI is built and made. In her view, utopia is not a destination but the “process of working together to develop a fairer world”. Maybe it would be unfair to expect too specific a utopian vision, but I’d nonetheless be interested to know how AI, specifically, can help us build a better future. She does not mention the things that many of AI’s biggest critics nonetheless welcome, such as its potential to improve drug discovery and disease detection. What if we got AI right, this book asks. After reading it, I can’t say I really know.
